verdict: Do not approve the active-active two-region project as proposed for next quarter. Re-scope it. First, fund targeted fixes for the failure modes the incident log actually shows: progressive/canary deploys with automated rollback, schema-migration and config validation, certificate auto-renewal and expiry monitoring, and a fallback for the third-party payment API. Second, treat region loss as a separate tail risk. Once the ledger's consistency model and RPO/RTO are defined, size a cheaper warm-standby or pilot-light DR option for it, and test that option against the SLA budget and the ledger RPO. The case for the project rests on three premises, and the evidence contradicts all three. (1) The contract target is 99.95% over a 30-day month, a budget of 21.6 min/month. It is not 99.99%, and 99.99% allows only 4.32 min/month, not about 52; 52.56 min is the yearly figure. (2) The 12-month log shows 0 region-wide outages. Bad deploys account for 92 of 115 customer-facing minutes (80%), and active-active would not clearly have prevented any of the 115 minutes. (3) The estimate requires 2 engineers for 2 quarters with the ledger consistency model still TBD, which conflicts with delivery next quarter. On a truncating reading of clause C.2, the two SLA misses (38 min in 2026-01, 22 min in 2026-08) triggered no service credit. Halvorsen's fees and termination terms are not in the packet, so the decision can only be bounded. Counting infrastructure cost only, here is one example of how avoided credits could pay for the project: a monthly fee of at least about $259k, with an uncapped, fully customer-facing outage on the scale of the 14.5h regional event avoided every year. At one such event every 5 years the fee would need to be about $1.29M/month. More frequent events, or multi-tier credits from shorter outages, would lower these fee thresholds. Relative to their cost and credit assumptions, the credit thresholds are lower bounds on the fee required. They exclude engineering cost, assume uncapped credits and full unavailability, and assume active-active would avoid the whole event. The packet does not establish, either way, whether a same-provider second region would have stayed available during a region-scoped event like Oct 2025. Customer-loss value cannot be bounded from the packet. As an illustrative point estimate only: if losing Halvorsen forfeited one year of contract value and the project prevented one such loss every 5 years (an arbitrary frequency, since the packet has no base rate), break-even contract value would be about $2.46M/yr. A multi-year remaining relationship would lower that figure, and counting margin instead of revenue would raise it. The recommendation rests on the target, root-cause and feasibility findings, not on these thresholds. It would change with the contract terms, a provider/region outage base rate, a ledger RPO requirement and internal cost estimates for the alternatives.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Poor fit. Bad deploys caused 92 of 115 customer-facing minutes (80%). Certificate expiry caused 11, the third-party payment API 9, and a single-AZ outage 3, which auto-failover already handled within one region. No minutes came from a region-wide outage. A second active region does not by itself prevent deploy, config, certificate or third-party failures.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Active-active protects against failures scoped to one region (loss of a region's infrastructure). Deploys, config pushes and certificates are usually shared across regions, so a bad change rolled out globally takes both regions down together. A third-party API outage is outside the company's regions entirely. Multi-region helps with change-induced failures only if rollouts are staged region by region with health gating. The same progressive-rollout and automated-rollback approach can be applied within one region, using canaries or cells, at much lower cost. External SRE material reports that change is the dominant cause of outages, which matches the log. At provider scale the same failure class appears. Google Cloud's June 2025 outage came from globally replicated policy metadata. Azure Front Door's Oct 2025 outage came from incompatible config metadata crashing edge servers globally. A second region at the same provider shares such global layers.
strengths: Would protect workloads against region-scoped infrastructure loss, a class of event that does occur (us-east-1 Oct 2025, ~14.5h window; Dec 2021, ~7h of Route 53 API impairment). It would not protect against dependencies on global control-plane functions anchored in the failed region. In Oct 2025, AWS status updates quoted by secondary outlets said such features 'may also be experiencing issues'.
Region-staged rollout across two regions could contain some bad deploys if adopted together with it
weaknesses: Leaves the dominant cause of downtime (bad deploys, 80% of minutes) untouched unless deploy practice also changes
The one infrastructure incident (single AZ, 3 min) was already mitigated in-region
0 region-wide outages affected the company in the 12-month log
Large recent provider outages spread through shared global layers (control planes, replicated config, global edge/DNS) that a same-provider second region does not remove

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The VP's arithmetic is wrong and the contract target is lower than the VP assumes. Over a 30-day month, 99.95% allows 21.6 min and 99.99% allows 4.32 min. The ~52.56 min figure is the yearly allowance at 99.99%. Against the 99.95% budget only two months missed: 2026-01 (38 min, ~99.912%) and 2026-08 (22 min, ~99.949%, over by 0.4 min). Adopting 99.99% would turn 6 of the 7 incident months into misses, since only the 3-minute month stays under 4.32 min.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Monthly budget = (1 - target) x 43,200 minutes in a 30-day month. Mixing up yearly and monthly allowances overstates the 99.99% budget by about 12x. Clause C.1 fixes the target at 99.95% over a 30-day month, excluding scheduled maintenance announced 72h ahead.
strengths: The contract target is directly verified from Schedule C
With the dominant failure modes reduced, the current 99.95% budget looks attainable without multi-region
weaknesses: The log has not been reconciled with the contract's measurement rules (definition of available, degraded states, maintenance exclusions), so the two misses may not be contractual breaches
The canonical SRE availability table could not be fetched; the arithmetic is standard and checked here independently

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Measured credit exposure has been small. On a truncating reading of C.2, the first 10% credit tier needs availability at or below 99.85%, which is 64.8 min of downtime in a 30-day month. The worst month was 38 min, so no credit appears to have been owed in the last 12 months. The real size of the risk (customer loss, termination for chronic breach) cannot be determined, because monthly fees, contract value and any termination or renewal terms are not in the packet. The sensitivity analysis below gives fee thresholds for the credit case and an illustrative figure for the churn case, to check against the actual contract.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Credits are a step function: 10% of monthly fees per full 0.1% below 99.95%. Small misses like 22 or 38 minutes fall below the first step, so routine credits are not the case for the project. The case rests on rare long outages and on customer loss. The excerpt shows no cap on credits. Suppose an outage the length of the Oct 2025 us-east-1 window (870 minutes) were entirely customer-facing in one 30-day month. Availability would then fall about 1.96 points below target, 19 full steps, or a 190% credit on that month's fee if uncapped. This is an upper-bound illustration: E10 reports three distinct impact periods with impact varying by service, and the company's provider and region are unknown. The sensitivity below uses infrastructure cost only ($492k/yr). (a) Credits: avoiding one 190% credit a year pays for the infrastructure only at a monthly fee of about $258.9k or more. At one such event every 5 years the fee would need to be about $1.29M/month. (b) Churn, illustrative only: if losing Halvorsen forfeits one year of contract value and the project prevented one such loss every 5 years, break-even contract value is about $2.46M/yr. Credit and churn values add, so a combination lowers each threshold. The credit thresholds in (a) are lower bounds in four respects. They exclude one engineer-year of loaded cost. They assume uncapped credits and full unavailability for the whole window. They assume active-active would have avoided the whole event. The packet does not establish whether a same-provider second region would have stayed available during a region-scoped event: E21 covers IAM updates and other control-plane functions, not other regions' data planes, and the E23/E24 global-layer outages are a different failure class. And they ignore cheaper hedges: if a warm standby recovered within 64.8 minutes, active-active would avoid almost no extra credit under the truncating reading. They are not bounds with respect to frequency, because more frequent events or multi-tier credits from shorter outages would lower them. The churn figure in (b) is not a bound. It is a point estimate under arbitrary assumptions. The 1-in-5-years frequency has no evidential base (E12). A multi-year remaining relationship would forfeit more than one year of value and lower the threshold in proportion. Counting margin rather than revenue would raise it. Chronic-breach risk is also not something active-active addresses, because the observed misses were deploy-caused. Credits could also offset the cost in other ways than one first-tier credit a month, for example through one long outage.
strengths: The credit mechanism is verified, so exposure for ordinary incidents can be bounded
Recent history suggests $0 in credits, on the truncating interpretation
Credit break-even thresholds give the decision-maker concrete fee levels to check against the actual contract
weaknesses: The fee amount is unknown, so dollar exposure cannot be computed, only bounded
No chronic-breach or termination terms are visible; relationship and renewal risk may outweigh credits
The churn break-even depends on remaining relationship length, margin and an arbitrary outage frequency, so it is illustrative only
How 'full 0.1%' is applied is inferred, not confirmed
There is no visible cap, so a long regional outage could produce a credit larger than a month's fee
The 870-minute illustration overstates likely impact, since E10 reports varying, partial impact

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The proposed spend is at least $492k/yr in infrastructure plus 2 engineers for 2 quarters (one engineer-year). It excludes ongoing operational overhead, licensing, and cross-region replication or data-transfer costs. Cheaper targeted measures address the 103 minutes from deploy and certificate causes directly. AWS DR guidance places warm standby and pilot light below active-active in cost and complexity as hedges against region loss. No company-specific cost figures exist for the alternatives, so the comparison is directional rather than quantified.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Cost-effectiveness depends on minutes avoided per dollar. The active-active project avoids roughly 0 of the observed minutes. Deploy safety and certificate automation target up to 103 of 115. For region loss, warm standby (RTO/RPO in minutes) trades a failover outage and, with async replication, a non-zero RPO for much lower steady-state cost than running two full active sites.
strengths: The platform estimate gives a clear infrastructure baseline ($41k/month)
AWS guidance (seen as search snippets) says active/active should only be selected when business requirements necessitate it
weaknesses: The TCO is understated: no loaded engineering cost, operational overhead or database replication costs
There are no internal estimates for the alternatives' cost or downtime reduction
The engineering cost in dollars cannot be computed from the packet

criteriaAssessments.assessment: High implementation risk. The ledger database needs multi-region writes, but its consistency model and RPO/RTO are 'TBD with product/finance'. Active-active writes on a financial ledger bring conflict, split-brain and latency risk. The 2-quarter engineering estimate conflicts with delivery next quarter.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Multi-leader writes make conflicting updates unavoidable. Ledger invariants spanning several records are among the hardest cases to reconcile. A two-site design without a third-location quorum or witness risks split-brain. Synchronous cross-region commit adds roughly 100-200 ms per write, from a low-authority source. The common pattern for ledgers is strong consistency with home-region routing, or active-passive. During migration, new failover and replication paths are new sources of change-induced outages, the very category that already dominates the log.
strengths: Defining the ledger RPO/RTO is useful whichever option is chosen
weaknesses: Consistency model undefined
Timeline not credible for next quarter
Risk of lowering availability during the transition
Sources on active-active conflict risk are low-authority snippets

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Region loss is a real low-probability, high-impact risk. Two multi-hour us-east-1 events are documented (Oct 2025 ~14.5h window; Dec 2021 ~7h of Route 53 API impairment). If such an event were fully customer-facing it would exceed the 21.6-minute monthly budget about 40 times over. A same-provider second region removes only the region-scoped part of this risk, for two reasons. During the Oct 2025 event, AWS status updates quoted by secondary outlets said global features relying on us-east-1 endpoints (IAM updates, DynamoDB Global Tables) 'may also be experiencing issues'. And the June 2025 Google Cloud and Oct 2025 Azure Front Door outages spread through globally replicated config and global edge layers. That justifies some regional DR, but not necessarily active-active, and not on the basis of this contract's routine SLA performance. The cheaper hedges have real downsides. They shorten a regional outage rather than prevent that month's SLA miss. With async replication they can lose recent ledger writes. They are only as good as their rehearsal. The provider and region in use, and any other-customer, sales or regulatory requirements, are unknown.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Expected loss = frequency x impact. Frequency is low and has no authoritative base rate. Impact is large because of the uncapped step credits and possible customer loss. Warm standby or pilot light cuts a long regional outage from hours to minutes or tens of minutes, but published end-to-end pilot-light figures conflict. One blog gives about 10-30 minutes, excluding human decision time and DB promotion. Study guides give 30-60 minutes or 1-4 hours. Warm standby sits at the low end. Neither side is authoritative, so the range stays unresolved until a rehearsal measures it. Against the budget: the upper part of the 10-30 minute range already exceeds 21.6 minutes. Up to 60 minutes stays under the 64.8-minute first credit tier, if nothing else happens that month. A 4-hour failover leaves availability about 0.51 points below target, 5 full steps or a 50% credit. On RPO, async cross-region replication loses unreplicated writes on unplanned failover. For Aurora Global Database that is typically seconds, with lag usually under 1 s. A newer 2026 guide describes unplanned failover with an explicit allow-data-loss flag, while an older AWS post said no managed unplanned failover existed. Both agree that unplanned failover on async replication accepts data loss. For a ledger that may mean losing acknowledged transactions. Synchronous replication to the standby, or a quorum database across three or more locations, gives RPO near zero at the cost of cross-region latency on every commit. Failover also depends on control planes (DNS changes, IAM, provisioning) that may be degraded during the very event. A rarely exercised standby needs regular drills to be trusted, and the cost of those drills is not in the packet.
strengths: Documented regional events show the risk is not hypothetical
Regional DR may serve other customers or future sales requirements
weaknesses: No base rate for the company's own provider and region
No evidence of other customers or regulations requiring active-active
Same-provider multi-region (active-active or standby) does not remove shared global dependencies
Warm standby/pilot light failover times are contested and come from low-authority sources; async standby implies RPO > 0 for the ledger

claims.text: The contract target is 99.95% availability per 30-day month, not 99.99%.

Over a 30-day month, 99.95% allows 21.6 minutes of downtime and 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes. The ~52.56 minutes at 99.99% is a yearly allowance, so the VP's 'about 52 minutes a month' is wrong by roughly 12x.
The 12-month log records 115 customer-facing minutes. Bad deploys caused 92 of them (80%), and region-wide outages caused 0.

Active-active across two regions would not clearly have prevented any of the 115 logged minutes. Deploy, config and certificate failures rolled out to both regions take both down. A third-party API outage is outside the regions. Auto-failover already contained the AZ event in-region.
Two months missed the 99.95% target: 2026-01 at ~99.912% (38 min) and 2026-08 at ~99.949% (22 min, over budget by 0.4 min).

On a truncating reading of C.2, the first credit tier needs at least 64.8 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month. No month reached that, so no service credit appears to have been owed in the last 12 months.
Annual incremental infrastructure cost is $492,000, plus 2 engineers for 2 quarters. Neither figure includes operational overhead or database replication costs.

As one example, credits could offset $41k/month of infrastructure if a first-tier (10%) credit occurred every month on a monthly fee of at least $410,000. Other patterns could offset it at lower fees or lower frequency, such as multi-tier credits or a single long outage (see CL17). This example excludes engineering cost.

The ledger consistency model and RPO/RTO are undefined, and the estimate needs 2 quarters of engineering. Completing the project next quarter is therefore not credible, and multi-region ledger writes carry conflict and split-brain risk.

Suppose a regional outage as long as the Oct 2025 us-east-1 window (~14.5h, 870 minutes) were entirely customer-facing in a 30-day month. It would exceed the 21.6-minute monthly budget about 40 times over and leave availability about 1.96 points below target: 19 full 0.1% credit steps, or 190% of that month's fee if uncapped. This is an upper-bound illustration. E10 reports three distinct impact periods with impact varying by service, and the company's provider and region are unknown.
AWS DR guidance places warm standby and pilot light below active/active in cost and complexity, and advises choosing active/active only when business requirements necessitate it.
The total financial exposure to Halvorsen cannot be determined: monthly fees, contract value, and any termination-for-chronic-breach or renewal terms are not in the supplied documents.
The annual probability of a full region outage at the company's provider and region cannot be determined from the packet, so expected regional-outage minutes cannot be quantified.
The cost and downtime reduction of the targeted alternatives cannot be quantified for this company, because no internal estimates exist.
It cannot be determined whether the logged minutes match the contract's availability measurement, so it is unconfirmed whether the 2026-01 and 2026-08 misses are contractual breaches.
Change-induced failures are the dominant cause of outages in external SRE experience as well, which supports prioritising deploy safety.

Sensitivity, using infrastructure cost only ($492k/yr). Avoiding one uncapped 19-step (190%) regional-outage credit per year breaks even at a monthly fee of about $258.9k. At one such event every 5 years the fee would need to be about $1.29M/month. Relative to their cost and credit assumptions, these credit thresholds are lower bounds on the fee required. They exclude engineering cost, assume uncapped credits and full unavailability, and assume active-active would avoid the whole event and that no cheaper hedge exists. Whether a same-provider second region would have stayed available during a region-scoped event like Oct 2025 is not established by the packet. More frequent events, or multi-tier credits from shorter outages, would lower the thresholds. Separately, as an illustrative point estimate and not a bound: if losing Halvorsen forfeits one year of contract value and the project prevented one such loss every 5 years, break-even contract value is about $2.46M/yr. The 5-year frequency is arbitrary, with no base rate in the packet. A multi-year remaining relationship would lower the figure in proportion, and counting margin rather than revenue would raise it. Whether the actual contract clears any of these cannot be determined from the packet.

Warm standby or pilot light shortens a regional outage but does not reliably keep that month within the SLA. Published pilot-light end-to-end figures range from about 10-30 minutes (one blog, excluding human decision time and DB promotion) to 30-60 minutes or 1-4 hours (study guides). The upper part of that range exceeds the 21.6-minute budget. Up to 60 minutes stays under the 64.8-minute first credit tier. A 4-hour failover leaves availability about 0.51 points below target, 5 full credit steps (50%). No authoritative measured end-to-end figure exists in the packet.

An asynchronously replicated standby has RPO above zero. For Aurora Global Database, data loss on failover depends on replication lag, typically seconds with lag usually under 1 s, and unplanned failover explicitly accepts losing unreplicated writes. For a financial ledger this may mean losing acknowledged transactions. Near-zero RPO requires synchronous replication (to a single-writer standby, or a quorum database across three or more locations), which adds cross-region latency to every commit. Having two active writers does not provide it.

Multi-region at a single provider does not protect against failures of shared global layers. Google Cloud's June 2025 outage came from globally replicated policy metadata, and Azure Front Door's Oct 2025 outage crashed edge servers globally. During the Oct 2025 us-east-1 event, AWS status updates, quoted by secondary outlets, said global features relying on us-east-1 endpoints (IAM updates, DynamoDB Global Tables) 'may also be experiencing issues'. That is a hedged status statement reached only through search snippets. The Oct 2025 trigger itself was regional (E10). The two accounts are compatible: the regional trigger impaired workloads in that region and may also have affected some global control-plane functions anchored there. The extent of data-plane impact in other regions is not established.

alternatives.option: Deploy safety: progressive/canary rollout, automated rollback, schema-migration discipline, config validation
alternatives.comparison: Targets the 92 of 115 minutes (80%) caused by bad deploys, which active-active does not address. It can be done in a single region. The packet has no company-specific cost, but it requires no duplicate infrastructure, unlike the $492k/yr in the proposal.
Targets the 11-minute certificate incident directly. Active-active would not help if certificates are shared across regions.

alternatives.option: Third-party payment API fallback (retry/queue, secondary provider or graceful degradation)
alternatives.comparison: Targets the 9-minute third-party incident, which lies outside the company's regions; active-active does nothing for it.

alternatives.option: Warm standby or pilot light DR in a second region
alternatives.comparison: Hedges the region-loss tail risk at lower cost and complexity than active/active, according to AWS DR guidance (snippet-level). It shortens rather than prevents that month's SLA miss. End-to-end failover ranges from about 10 minutes to hours depending on automation and rehearsal, so it can exceed the 21.6-minute budget and, at the slow end, the 64.8-minute credit tier. It keeps the ledger single-writer, which avoids multi-writer conflicts. With async replication, though, RPO is above zero (typically seconds), so recent ledger writes can be lost on unplanned failover unless synchronous replication is paid for in commit latency. It needs regular failover drills, and failover can depend on control planes degraded during the same event.

Gives near-zero RTO for region-scoped loss. It costs at least $492k/yr plus one engineer-year, removes approximately none of the observed minutes, does not remove shared global-layer dependencies at the same provider, and carries ledger consistency risk with an undefined RPO/RTO.

alternatives.option: Defer the decision pending contract terms and ledger RPO/RTO
alternatives.comparison: Costs little, and it closes the main unknowns (fees, termination terms, provider base rate). Deploy-safety work should not wait for this.

tradeoffs: Near-zero regional RTO (active-active) against far lower cost and complexity with a failover outage of minutes to hours (warm standby or pilot light), which may still breach that month's 21.6-minute budget. With async replication the standby also has a non-zero ledger RPO, unless synchronous replication is paid for in commit latency.
Spending on the observed dominant risk (deploys) against the unobserved but high-impact tail risk (region loss)
Strong ledger consistency against multi-region write availability: active-active ledgers must accept conflict handling or added cross-region latency
Engineering capacity: one engineer-year on multi-region is capacity not spent on deploy safety, which addresses 80% of minutes
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: A global config or deploy push reaches both active regions at once, causing a two-region outage despite the spend
Split-brain on the ledger in a two-site design without a third-location witness, producing conflicting financial records
Failover or replication-lag bugs introduced during migration add new change-induced outages in the transition period

Shared global layers fail and impair several regions at once. Google Cloud's June 2025 outage spread through globally replicated policy metadata. Azure Front Door's Oct 2025 outage crashed edge servers globally. In the Oct 2025 us-east-1 event, AWS status updates quoted by secondary outlets said global features relying on us-east-1 endpoints (IAM updates, DynamoDB Global Tables) 'may also be experiencing issues'. A second region at the same provider shares these dependencies.

A rarely exercised standby or failover path fails when needed, or the failover depends on control planes (DNS record changes, IAM, provisioning) that are degraded during the same event; in Dec 2021, Route 53 APIs were impaired for about 7 hours
Unplanned failover on async replication discards unreplicated ledger writes (RPO above zero), leaving acknowledged transactions missing after failover
A single long regional outage in a month leaves availability far below target; with no visible credit cap, credits could exceed the month's fee
Log minutes may undercount contractual downtime, e.g. degraded-but-up states, or overcount it, e.g. maintenance exclusions, changing the breach history
Calendar-month incidents that span a month boundary could be attributed differently under the 30-day measurement basis

counterarguments.argument: Zero regional outages in 12 months does not mean the risk is low; regional outages are rare but catastrophic.
counterarguments.response: Agreed that the tail risk is real: a 14.5h event, if fully customer-facing, would exceed the monthly budget about 40x. But it argues for regional DR sized to a defined RTO and RPO, not specifically for active-active. AWS DR guidance ranks warm standby and pilot light below active/active in cost and complexity, and in one worked example finds them sufficient; this is snippet-level evidence. A standby shortens the breach rather than avoiding it, since failover ranges from about 10 minutes to hours. Recent large outages also spread through global layers that active-active at the same provider would share.

counterarguments.argument: Active-active with region-by-region staged deploys would also contain bad deploys.
counterarguments.response: True only if staged rollout is adopted, and staged rollout with health gating and automated rollback can be done within one region at much lower cost. The containment comes from the deploy practice, not from the second active region.

counterarguments.argument: The largest customer may expect 99.99% regardless of the contract, or the VP may intend 99.99% as an internal SLO that leaves headroom under the 99.95% SLA.
counterarguments.response: An internal SLO tighter than the SLA is sound practice, and current headroom is thin: 2026-08 missed by only 0.4 minutes. But a 99.99% SLO (4.32 min/month) would have been missed in 6 of 7 incident months. All of those misses had causes multi-region does not remove, so the headroom has to come from cutting deploy minutes. The verified contract says 99.95%, and no evidence in the packet shows a 99.99% requirement from this or any other customer.

counterarguments.argument: Credits may be computed non-truncated, so past misses may have cost money.
counterarguments.response: Possible: the interpretation of C.2 is inferred. Even so, the misses were 16.4 and 0.4 minutes over budget, both deploy-caused, so the fix they argue for is deploy safety, not multi-region.

counterarguments.argument: An async-replicated standby can lose committed ledger transactions on failover, and only active-active gives near-zero RPO.
counterarguments.response: It is correct that async standby RPO is above zero (typically seconds), and for a ledger that may be unacceptable. But zero RPO comes from synchronous replication, not from having two active writers. Multi-leader async active-active also loses unreplicated writes and adds conflicts. Synchronous replication to a single-writer standby, or a quorum database across three or more locations, gives near-zero RPO at the cost of cross-region latency per commit. The ledger RPO is still TBD. If product/finance require zero loss, either design must be priced with synchronous replication.

furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion: Contract terms showing termination for chronic breach, a 99.99% commitment, or high fees with uncapped credits could raise the value of regional resilience.
